acceptedAnswer.text: PDFree encrypts your PDF with RC4-128 — the PDF format's Revision 3 standard security handler (PDF 1.4–1.7). It requires your password to open in Adobe Acrobat, Preview, and every standard-compliant PDF reader. Note this is not AES-256: for regulated or extremely sensitive documents, pair it with an additional safeguard rather than relying on it alone.

name: Does PDFree store or log my files after processing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. PDFree runs entirely in your browser — there is no backend server that receives your files. Because nothing is uploaded, nothing can be stored, logged, or retained. Your document exists only in your browser's memory for the duration of the session and is cleared when you close the tab.

A strong, unique password (12+ characters, mixed case, numbers, symbols) resists casual and automated cracking attempts. RC4-128 is weaker than modern ciphers like AES-256, so treat it as one layer of protection rather than your only safeguard for highly sensitive or regulated files.

name: Can I remove the password from a protected PDF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — upload the encrypted PDF, enter the current password, leave the new password field empty, and save. This produces an unprotected version of the file.

name: Will the password-protected PDF open in Adobe Reader?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. PDFree produces standard-compliant encrypted PDFs that open in Adobe Acrobat, Adobe Reader, macOS Preview, and all modern PDF viewers.

name: Is it safe to set the password on PDFree's website?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The entire encryption process runs in your browser — your password and document are never transmitted to any server. PDFree literally cannot see them.

name: Can I set different passwords for opening and editing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. You can set an owner password (for editing/printing restrictions) separately from a user password (for opening the file).

name: Can I password-protect multiple PDF files at once?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. PDFree's batch mode lets you add a password and permissions to many PDF files in one pass — select or drag in multiple files, and each is encrypted separately in your browser with the same settings. You'll get a ZIP with all protected files, and nothing is ever uploaded to a server.

name: Is RC4-128 encryption safe enough to protect a PDF?

acceptedAnswer.text: For everyday use — keeping a document private from casual access, sharing sensitive files with people you trust, or restricting printing/copying — yes, RC4-128 is a real, working PDF standard supported since PDF 1.4 that every reader can open. It's not as strong as AES-256, though, and a well-resourced attacker with the encrypted file could break it. For medical records, legal filings, or anything with real regulatory stakes, don't rely on password protection alone — combine it with an encrypted drive, a secure file-sharing service, or your organization's own compliance tooling. One advantage RC4-128 does have: it opens in older PDF readers that don't support AES-256 at all, so a password-protected PDF you send stays openable for the widest range of recipients.
